And there is real truth in it, because Jesus does not leave our behavior alone. He plainly calls his followers to obey him, to turn from sin, to live differently, and a Christianity that asks nothing of how you actually live has edited out half the New Testament. The second error says the opposite, that following is only about being loved and accepted, that since grace is free and the love is unconditional, nothing is really required and nothing actually needs to change. And there is genuine truth here too, the most precious truth there is, because the love did come first, before you cleaned up anything, and you cannot earn it by your behavior or lose it by your failure. Now watch both fall, and watch the order, because the order is the entire gospel. Following is not first about behavior, which corrects the moralist, because if you put the behavior first you get the most poisonous reversal in all of religion, the idea that you change in order to be loved. Get the order backward and you produce either despair, when you cannot change enough, or pride, when you think you have. The gospel runs the other way. The love came first. You were accepted before you were improved, and the change grows out of the love rather than purchasing it. But following is also not a love that leaves you unchanged, which corrects the cheap-grace error, because a love that meets a person and leaves them exactly as it found them is not the love the New Testament describes. Think about what any great love does. When a person genuinely falls in love, their whole life rearranges, the calendar, the spending, the priorities, the habits, not because a rulebook landed on the table demanding it, but because a person arrived and everything reorganized itself around the new center. That is the change Jesus is after. Not behavior modification to earn his favor, but the natural reordering of a life that now has a new center of gravity. So let me give you the two words the church has always used, and let me clean the dread off them. Repentance. It sounds like groveling, but it simply means turning, changing direction, and it is not a one-time entry fee you paid at the start. It is a direction you keep turning, daily, for the rest of your life, every time you notice you have drifted. And obedience. It sounds like a boot on your neck, but it is not the rent you pay to stay loved. It is the shape a reordered life naturally takes, the way you find yourself wanting to live once the new center has moved in. Here is the hard honesty, though, and a new believer needs it now rather than later. You will keep failing. You will discover, often in the first months, sins you never noticed before, and you will turn from the same things over and over and wonder whether the change ever really took. It took. The fact that you keep having to turn is not evidence of fraud, it is evidence of life, because dead things do not struggle and living things do. And here is the turn that ends the whole study, the thing I most need you to carry out of this room. You were never meant to walk this road on your own willpower, gritting your teeth up the hill toward a holiness you manufacture by trying harder. That road kills people, or it makes Pharisees of them. You walk this road with Christ himself, and he is not standing at the finish line with a stopwatch, disappointed in your pace. He is on the road, beside you, walking it with you, the same gentle Companion the whole way, and he has promised to finish what he started, which means the completion of you is finally his responsibility and not yours alone. And I will not pretend to you, from some imagined summit, that I have arrived, because I have not. I am decades into this now, and I still repent of things I repented of at the very beginning. I have found the road far longer than I thought it would be when I first stepped onto it from atheism, certain it would all be sorted in a year or two. And I have found the Companion far kinder than I had any reason to expect, kinder the longer I walk and the more of myself I see. So this study does not end with a bow, because the Christian life does not get a bow this side of heaven. It ends the way it should end, with a road stretching out ahead of you, longer than you hoped, and a Companion beside you, gentler than you feared, who knew exactly what he was getting when he took you, and took you anyway, and will not leave the road until you are home. You have not arrived. You are not finished. You do not need to be. You only need to take the next step, and to take it with him.

scriptureStudy.note: If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. Following is daily and lifelong, a road walked behind a Person, not a single completed decision, which sets honest expectations for the long stretch.

Work out your own salvation, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work. The effort is real, but the power underneath it is God's own working, so obedience is response and participation, never self-manufactured.

God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance. The order is named directly, kindness comes first and leads to the turning, never the turning earning the kindness, which is the whole architecture of the gospel.

If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, but if we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive. Ongoing confession is assumed for real believers, so still having sin to confess is normal walking, not proof the new birth failed.

The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience. Real change is described as fruit that grows, slow and organic and produced by the Spirit, not as behavior bolted on by willpower to earn acceptance.

Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith. The race is long and needs endurance, and the eyes stay on Jesus who both begins and completes the faith, not on our own performance.

He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. The same promise that opened the study closes it, the completion is Christ's responsibility, which is why the unfinished road is not cause for despair.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the church's long teaching on sanctification, the unglamorous word for the lifelong process by which a believer is actually changed, because the new believer needs to know that the gap between being declared right with God and feeling fully changed is not a defect in their experience but the normal architecture of the Christian life. The tradition has carefully distinguished justification, the once-for-all declaration that a person stands accepted by God on the basis of Christ's work and not their own, from sanctification, the slow ongoing work of the Spirit conforming that person to Christ over a lifetime, and it has insisted the first grounds the second rather than the reverse, that we are changed because we are accepted, never accepted because we are changed. This guards two cliffs. On one side, the moralism that collapses acceptance into performance and leaves a believer forever anxious about whether they have done enough, which is why the order in this session matters so much. On the other side, the antinomian error that, seizing on free grace, concludes that since acceptance is unearned, growth is optional and sin no longer matters, which the New Testament flatly rejects. Set this beside the modern impatience for instant transformation, the cultural expectation that real change should be fast and visible and complete, and ask what damage that does to a believer being changed at the slow pace of an actual human life. A serious group should weigh how to hold assurance and effort together, resting fully in an acceptance already secured while genuinely pressing on in obedience, neither earning what is given nor neglecting what is grown, and should recover the patience the older writers had with their own slow progress, the willingness to walk a long road with a Christ who is both the one who declares them righteous now and the one who is patiently making them so.

memoryVerse.text: And he said to all, If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.

leaderPrimer: Leading this study is closer to holding a newborn than to teaching a class, and the first mistake is the one most natural to people who have believed a long time. We bury the beginning in vocabulary. Justification, sanctification, quiet time, walking with the Lord, all the shorthand that took us twenty years to stop noticing lands on a two-week-old faith like a load on a seedling, and the new believer concludes that everyone else got a manual and they missed the day it was handed out. Watch your language like a guard at a gate, and watch the altitude of the room even harder, because the well-meaning veteran who wandered in will want to raise controversies and correct wording, and their knowledge is real but their timing is wrong. Keep the room at the level of first steps, kindly and firmly. The order you must guard above everything is the order of the gospel itself. Love first, then everything else. The reading, the praying, the belonging, the turning, all of it grows out of a love already given, and none of it earns or keeps that love. If this study becomes a checklist a beginner performs to feel acceptable, you will have rebuilt the exact religion the gospel came to end. Then normalize the beginning, more times than feels necessary, because shame is loud. The high that faded was weather, not the thing itself. The sins they keep discovering mean they are awake, not failing. Nobody knows how to pray at first, including the twelve, which is why they asked. Bell learned these steps with no map at all. He came from atheism, no childhood church, no warm memory, no one to teach him, and he took the first steps clumsily and often wrongly, which is why this study assumes nothing and shames nothing. There will likely be a seeker at your table too, not yet believing, watching to see what they would be signing up for. Do not recruit them. Let them ask their hardest questions and find the questions welcome. When you pray to close each night, pray plainly, short and true and unembarrassed, because they are learning what ordinary prayer sounds like from your mouth. The fifth session ends on a road, not an arrival. Send them out walking, unfinished, accompanied. That is the truest thing you can give them.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me perform or prove my faith before I am ready?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that. The whole study insists on the order, that the love came first and the change grows out of it, never the other way around, and it tells leaders to say that out loud more than once. You are not reading the Bible, praying, finding a church, or turning from sin in order to earn God's love or keep it. The love was already given before you cleaned up anything. The first session even reassures you that the fading of the initial feeling does not mean the thing was not real, and the last session tells you plainly that still struggling with the same sins is evidence of life, not of fraud. If you came braced to be put on a treadmill of religious performance, you will find instead a study built to take the weight off, and a leader primer that warns the facilitator never to turn these practices into a checklist for feeling acceptable.

faq.q: What if I do not feel anything anymore? The first weeks were powerful and now I feel nothing. Was it real?
faq.a: It was almost certainly real, and the first session is built around exactly this fear. The feeling you had was real and good, but the new birth was never a feeling, it was something God did, and feelings are weather, they roll in and roll out while the fact of what happened holds. Scripture does not say you are saved as long as the glow lasts. It says you were born again, and a newborn does not stop being alive when the thrilling morning of its birth is over. The study points out that the writer, who came to faith from atheism, did not feel joy the morning he could no longer deny Christ, he felt fear, and he was as born again that frightened morning as ever since. Your assurance was never meant to rest on your mood. It rests on what God did, and God does not undo a birth because the baby is having a hard week.

faq.q: I tried to read the Bible and got completely lost. Am I just not smart enough or spiritual enough for it?
faq.a: No, you simply did what nearly every beginner does and started on page one, which strands most people in the ancient laws. The Bible is not one book to read front to back, it is a library of sixty-six books written across centuries, and the second session tells you to start somewhere else entirely, with Mark, the shortest account of the life of Jesus, one chapter a day. The whole library has one person at its center, and you read to meet him first, after which the rest slowly makes sense. The first habit is the plainest one, ask what the passage says before you ask what it means for you. The failure you experienced was a method problem, not a soul problem, and the study even points you to a plain step-by-step way to read and a tool for looking up any passage when you get curious.

faq.q: I do not know how to pray and I feel like I am doing it wrong. What is the secret?
faq.a: There is no secret and no special language, and the third session exists to free you from the fear that there is. When Jesus' own friends asked him to teach them to pray, he told them to begin with one word, Father, the plainest word a small child has, which means the whole premise that you need fluency is false. Prayer is honest speech toward a Father who already knows everything you are about to say and stayed anyway. Short and true beats long and impressive, because God is not grading the grammar. The disciples who walked with Jesus daily still had to ask him how, so not knowing is where everyone starts, not a disqualification. And if you are not even sure anyone is listening, the study says you may pray that too, out loud to God, because some of the realest prayers in the Bible are people telling God they are unsure he is there.

faq.q: I love Jesus but I am done with church. Why does this study say I cannot follow alone?
faq.a: Because the New Testament cannot even imagine a solo Christian, and the fourth session takes your wound seriously while refusing the conclusion. If you were hurt by a church, that hurt is real and the study does not wave it off, and it does not tell you to return to the place that wounded you. But the just me and Jesus plan removes the very place faith is meant to grow, because nearly everything Christ commands, forgive one another, bear one another's burdens, love one another, is impossible to practice alone. The church is not a building or a brand you consume, the word means the people, a family. You are not looking for a perfect church, there is no such thing, only a place where the Bible is taken seriously and the people are honest about needing grace. The writer, who came in as an outsider, says the ordinary kindness of flawed church people was the proof of the gospel he could not argue away.

faq.q: Does following Jesus eventually just turn into a list of rules I have to keep?
faq.a: No, and the fifth session names this fear directly and answers it with the order, which is everything. You do not obey to keep God happy with you. God was already for you, the love came first, before you changed a single thing, and nothing you do or stop doing earns it or loses it. Obedience is not the rent you pay to stay loved, it is the way a reordered life naturally arranges itself once a new center has moved in, the way anyone in love finds their whole life rearranging around the person, not because a rulebook arrived but because a person did. Repentance is not a one-time entry fee but a direction you keep turning your whole life. The change is real and following genuinely costs everything, but it is the cost of love reordering a life, not a treadmill of demands. Get the order backward and you are right to dread it. Get it right and it stops being a list and becomes a life.

faq.q: I keep failing at the same things even after coming to Jesus. Does that mean I am a fraud?
faq.a: No, it means you are on the road and not at the end of it, which is where every honest Christian who has ever lived has been. The fifth session is blunt about this because it drives so many new believers back out the door. Repentance is a direction, a daily turning, not a one-time fee you paid and failed to honor, and the fact that you keep having to turn from the same things is the normal experience of being changed slowly over years rather than instantly overnight. The writer says plainly that decades in he still repents of the same things he repented of at the beginning. The goal was never to be sinless by next week. It is a life pointed in a new direction, turning again whenever it drifts, carried by a Christ who knew exactly what he was getting when he took you and took you anyway. You are not a fraud. You are a beginner, on a long road, with a patient Companion.

faq.q: Can a seeker who is not sure they believe yet come to this study?
faq.a: Yes, and the study is deliberately built with room for exactly that person. The writer came to faith from atheism, opening a Bible to disprove it, so the study takes honest doubt seriously rather than treating it as a problem to fix by the end of the night. The leader primer tells the facilitator not to pressure or single out the seeker, to let them ask their hardest questions, and to make the room the safest place a doubter has ever sat. You are allowed to say I am not sure I believe this and be met with welcome rather than anxious persuasion. The session on prayer even tells you that you may pray your doubt out loud to God, and the session on the Bible invites you to keep your hard questions and write them down while you read. Some things, the study keeps saying, are only learned from the inside, so a seeker is welcome to look from the inside while they decide.

faq.q: Do I have to have a dramatic testimony for my conversion to count?
faq.a: No, and the first session works to free you from exactly that comparison. New believers measure themselves against the dramatic stories they have heard and conclude their own quieter or stranger beginning does not count. But the new birth is something God did, not a feeling you produced or a cinematic moment you staged, and it does not require goosebumps or tears to be real. The writer's own beginning, coming out of atheism, was not a warm or joyful scene, it was frightened and full of grief for a certainty he was losing, and it was as real a new birth as any. The study asks you to write the plainest account you can of what actually happened, in your own words, with no borrowed language, precisely so you stop performing someone else's testimony and own your own. What makes it count is not the drama. It is what God did.

faq.q: Why does the study keep bringing up that the writer was an atheist?
faq.a: Because it is the method, and the method is the welcome. Bell does not stand outside the beginning as the expert explaining the basics to novices. He came to faith from atheism, with no Christian background and no childhood church, and he had to learn the first steps himself, clumsily and often wrongly, with no one to teach him. He knows the fear of opening a Bible and understanding nothing, the embarrassment of not knowing how to pray, the temptation to follow alone, the morning he could no longer deny Christ and felt terror rather than joy. He writes from inside the beginning, not above it, and the study asks every leader to do the same, because you cannot welcome someone into something you are pretending you never had to find your own way into. A leader who can say I am also a beginner, still turning, still unsure, can walk beside a new believer as a fellow traveler, which is the only place real encouragement comes from.

faq.q: Does this study promise that following Jesus will be easy or make my problems go away?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to. The study is honest that following costs everything, that the road is long, that you will keep failing and turning, that the church will sometimes wound you, and that hard questions will not all be answered on schedule. The fifth session ends on purpose with a road stretching out ahead rather than a finish line, because the Christian life does not get a tidy resolution this side of heaven. What the study promises is not an easy life or a quick arrival but a Companion for the long walk, a Christ who came first with love, who walks the road beside you, and who has promised to finish what he started. The point is not the absence of struggle but the presence of the One walking through it with you, gentler the longer you walk, who knew exactly what he was getting when he took you and took you anyway.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I am still pretty new myself, or still struggle with the basics?
faq.a: Being new is not a disqualification. It may be your single greatest qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow beginner, not by an expert who has it all figured out, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about your own clumsy beginning, your own unanswered questions, your own ongoing turning from the same old things, may be the most encouraging thing in the room, the permission that lets others stop performing a mastery no one actually has. What you do need is to get the order right and guard it, love before change always, to normalize the small frightened beginning so no one is ashamed of it, to keep the room safe for the wounded and welcoming for the doubter, and to point everyone, yourself first, toward the One who said follow me. Read the leader primer, remember your own beginning, and trust the material.

timeline.event: Jesus calls his first disciples with two words, follow me, beginning the pattern of discipleship as a walk behind a Person rather than the mastery of a system, the pattern the fifth session rests on.

Jesus tells Nicodemus by night that he must be born again, born from above, naming the change at the center of the Christian life as a birth received rather than a self-improvement achieved, the ground of the first session.

The disciples, having watched Jesus pray, ask him to teach them how, and he answers with the short, plain prayer that begins with the word Father, setting prayer as a child's speech to a parent rather than a performance in a special language.

At Pentecost the first community is formed, devoting itself to the teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers, and holding life in common, establishing from the start that the faith is lived as a people and not alone.

Paul writes letters to young churches full of brand new believers, addressing them not as finished saints but as people being slowly changed, grounding every command in the grace already given, modeling the order the fifth session insists on.

Peter writes that believers have been born again of imperishable seed and are now a chosen people, a royal priesthood, naming both the new birth and the new corporate identity that the first and fourth sessions explore.

Cyprian of Carthage gives voice to the early conviction that the Christian cannot have God as Father who will not have the church as mother, a strong early statement of the truth that following was never designed to be solitary.
Augustine, himself a dramatic late convert from a worldly life, writes his Confessions, modeling the honest account of a beginning and the slow lifelong reordering of a life around a new center.

The Reformers recover the conviction that a believer can know they belong to Christ, resting assurance on God's finished work rather than on the believer's shifting feelings, the very ground the first session offers the anxious new believer.

John Bunyan publishes The Pilgrim's Progress, picturing the Christian life as a long road walked with companions through real danger toward a city, the enduring image behind the fifth session's road that does not end at a quick arrival.

C. S. Lewis, who came to faith from atheism as an adult, has by now published Mere Christianity's earliest broadcasts and his account of a reluctant, reasoned conversion, a modern witness that one can arrive at faith from unbelief and learn the first steps late.

Eugene Peterson begins the pastoral writing that will become A Long Obedience in the Same Direction, recovering for a hurried age the truth that discipleship is a long, slow, ordinary faithfulness rather than a burst of intensity, anchoring the fifth session's vision of the long road.

Dane Ortlund publishes Gentle and Lowly, drawing the church's attention to the heart of Christ toward sinners and sufferers as gentle and lowly, the very kindness the fifth session promises the new believer will find growing along the long road.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and a special welcome to anyone for whom this is brand new, or anyone still deciding what they believe. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say I do not understand here. You can say I am not sure I believe this here. Nobody is going to pressure you or quiz you or expect you to perform a faith you do not have. Second, everything we talk about runs on grace, which is the old word for love you did not earn and cannot pay back. You are not here to prove anything or to earn anything. The love came first, and everything else grows out of it. Third, the writer of this study came to faith from atheism, with no church background and no head start, and he had to learn all of this the hard way, so we are not experts teaching beginners. We are all beginners, and I will go first whenever it counts. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones, and not knowing is a perfectly good place to start.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the ordinary week ahead, into the actual mornings and the real decisions, because that is where the first steps are either taken or not. Nobody here is expected to have arrived. We are just taking the next small step, together.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not all wrapped up, because following Jesus is a long road and not a quick arrival, and pretending otherwise would not help you. Take one small step this week rather than trying to do everything at once. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. If you have a hard question that did not get answered tonight, that is fine, write it down and keep it, because some things are learned slowly, from the inside, as you walk. Let me pray for us before we go, plainly and briefly, the way we talked about, because that is what ordinary honest prayer sounds like. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this room, especially if all of this is new.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and grace, welcome any seekers plainly, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Name that the beginning is allowed to be small.
Week 2: Session 1, What Just Happened to Me, full discussion and practice on the new birth and assurance.
Week 3: Session 2, The Word, and How to Read It, with extended time on starting in Mark and the habit of asking what does it say.
Week 4: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father, part one through Father and the freedom from special language.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, short and true prayer, praying the doubt, and honest time for those unsure anyone is listening.
Week 6: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone, taking wounds seriously and the search for an imperfect but faithful church.
Week 7: Session 5, Following, the Long Road, the order of love before change and repentance as a lifelong direction.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and build the small rule of life card together, with space for anyone moved to take a next step into baptism or membership.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, what just happened and how to read the Bible, starting in Mark.
Week 2: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father, with extended time on praying plainly and praying the doubt.
Week 3: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone, the wound taken seriously and the imperfect church.
Week 4: Session 5, Following, the Long Road, plus a short integration close and the building of the small rule of life card.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, What Just Happened to Me.
Week 2: Session 2, The Word, and How to Read It.
Week 3: Session 3, Prayer, Talking with the Father.
Week 4: Session 4, The Church, You Cannot Follow Alone.
Week 5: Session 5, Following, the Long Road.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The classic reasoned case for the faith by a man who came to it from atheism, warm and plain, useful for the seeker in the room and for the first session's treatment of conversion from unbelief.

bibliography.title: A Long Obedience in the Same Direction
bibliography.author: Eugene Peterson
bibliography.note: On discipleship as a slow, ordinary, lifelong faithfulness rather than a burst of intensity. The pastoral spine of session 5 and the long road.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: Draws out the gentle and lowly heart of Christ toward the struggling, the kindness the new believer will find along the road. Anchors the tone of session 5.

bibliography.title: Basic Christianity
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: A clear, unhurried introduction to who Christ is and what it means to follow him, written for inquirers and new believers. Useful across all five sessions. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
bibliography.author: John Bunyan
bibliography.note: The enduring allegory of the Christian life as a long road walked with companions toward a city, the image behind session 5's refusal of a quick arrival.

bibliography.title: Knowing God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: On the heart of the faith as knowing God personally rather than merely knowing about him, supporting the second session's aim of reading the Bible to meet a person. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: How to Read the Bible Book by Book
bibliography.author: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart
bibliography.note: A practical guide to reading Scripture as the kind of writing each book actually is, supporting session 2's method of starting in Mark and asking what the text says. Offered as a balancing voice on method.

bibliography.title: The Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The model of an honest account of a beginning and the slow reordering of a life around a new center, background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: On the gift and reality of Christian community, refusing both the idealized fantasy of perfect fellowship and the isolation that starves faith. Anchors session 4 on the church. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as the study's position.

bibliography.title: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A grounded treatment of prayer as relationship rather than technique, useful for session 3. Not cited by Bell directly. Leader to confirm before attributing specific claims.

bibliography.title: Celebration of Discipline
bibliography.author: Richard Foster
bibliography.note: An introduction to the ordinary practices that sustain a faith over years, supporting session 5's small rule of life. Offered as a balancing voice. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as Bell's own argument.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God: Belief in an Age of Skepticism
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Takes the doubter's hard questions seriously rather than waving them off, useful for the seeker in the room and for the honest questions raised in sessions 1 and 2. Leader to confirm specifics before attributing them to Bell.

furtherReading: Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis, for the seeker and for anyone wanting a plain reasoned account of the faith from a man who arrived at it from atheism.
A Long Obedience in the Same Direction, Eugene Peterson, for new believers who need the vision of discipleship as a slow lifelong faithfulness rather than a burst of intensity, anchoring session 5.
Basic Christianity, John Stott, for an unhurried introduction to who Christ is and what following him means, useful for the recently baptized, leader to confirm specific claims.
Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for anyone wrestling with session 4, on real Christian community that refuses both the perfect-church fantasy and the isolation that starves faith.
The Reason for God, Timothy Keller, for the doubter who wants their hard questions taken seriously rather than waved away, read alongside the study's welcome of honest questions.

glossary.definition: The old word for love you did not earn and cannot pay back. The whole Christian life begins and runs on it. You are not loved because you changed, you change because you are loved, and getting that order right is the heart of the study.

Jesus' word to Nicodemus for what happens at conversion, being born again, born from above. It names the change as something God does to a person rather than a self-improvement they achieve, which is why assurance rests on God's work and not on the believer's feeling.

The settled knowledge that you belong to Christ, meant to be possessed rather than endlessly chased. It rests first on what God has done and not on the weather of your emotions, which rise and fall while the fact of the new birth holds.

The old word means good news, and it is news rather than advice, the announcement of what God has done in Christ for people who could not do it for themselves. Everything the new believer is asked to do is a response to this news, never a way of earning it.

The long, slow learning to live as a student of Jesus, walked over years rather than completed at the start. It is following a Person down a road, not mastering a system, which is why the beginning is allowed to be small.

The shortest of the four Gospels, the four accounts of the life of Jesus, and the recommended place for a new believer to begin reading, one chapter at a time, to meet the person at the center of the whole Bible before tackling the rest of the library.

Honest speech toward a Father who already knows everything you are about to say and stayed anyway. It requires no special language and no minimum performance, since Jesus taught his friends to begin with the plainest word a child has, Father.

Not a building or a brand, but the people, a body, a family of ordinary and imperfect believers you belong to. The New Testament word means the called-out ones, and it assumes that following Jesus is something done with and for others, never alone.

Not groveling and not a one-time entry fee, but turning, changing direction. It is a daily, lifelong direction the believer keeps choosing whenever they drift, so still having things to turn from is the normal experience of a living faith, not proof of fraud.

Not the rent paid to stay loved, but the natural shape a reordered life takes once a new center has moved in. Like the way any great love rearranges a life, it flows out of the love already given rather than working to earn it.

The unglamorous word for the lifelong process by which a believer is actually changed and slowly conformed to Christ. It is grounded in an acceptance already secured, never the means of earning that acceptance, and it moves at the slow pace of a real human life.

The once-for-all declaration that a person stands accepted by God on the basis of Christ's work and not their own. It grounds all the change that follows, so the believer is changed because they are accepted, never accepted because they are changed.

The old word for telling God the truth when things hurt, honest and unedited. Scripture is full of it, which is why a new believer may bring their grief, their anger, and even their doubt to God in prayer rather than editing those things out.

Not a list of rules but a small set of chosen practices, a trellis, that holds a life up so it can grow in one direction over years. The new believer builds one small enough to keep on their worst week, from the practices that actually helped.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Something real happened, and nobody handed you a manual. This five-session study, written for the brand new Christian and the recently baptized, walks slowly through the first steps of following Jesus. What just happened to you and how you can know it was real. How to read the Bible without drowning on page one. How to pray when you do not know how. Why you cannot follow alone. And what the long road of following actually looks like over years. It runs on grace from start to finish, never loads a beginner with rules, and welcomes the seeker who is still deciding. Written by a man who came to faith from atheism and had to learn the first steps himself. Come new. Come unsure. Come honest.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study called The First Steps, written for anyone who has recently come to faith, been baptized, or is simply wondering what following Jesus would mean. It covers what happened to you, how to read the Bible, how to pray, how to find your people, and the long road ahead, all in plain words with every old church term defined. The writer came to faith from atheism, so the doubters are welcome too. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. If you are new to all this, or thinking about it, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: The new birth is not finally a feeling. Feelings are weather. The thing God did does not evaporate when Tuesday is gray.
Do not start the Bible at page one. Start with Mark, and read to meet the person at the center.
When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, he gave them one word to start with. Father.
Short and true beats long and impressive. God is not grading the grammar.
You are not looking for a perfect church. If you found one, your joining would ruin it.
The just me and Jesus plan removes the very place faith was built to grow.
You do not change in order to be loved. You change because you already are. Get the order right.
He is not standing at the finish line judging your pace. He is on the road, beside you, the whole way.
